topic: Why onions make you cry: tear gas from cut cells, eye nerves, chilling tip

slides.title: Cutting starts it
slides.body: Slicing breaks onion cells. Their enzymes mix and make a sulfur gas that drifts up toward your face.
slides.image_prompt: Halved red onion on a wooden cutting board beside a sharp knife, faint mist rising from the cut surface, soft kitchen light

slides.title: Your eyes fight back
slides.body: The gas hits the surface of your eyes. Nerves sense the irritation and your tear glands flush it away.
slides.image_prompt: Glistening water droplets on fresh onion rings, macro shot, shallow depth of field, cool morning light

slides.title: How to cry less
slides.body: A chilled onion can release less gas. A sharp knife crushes fewer cells, so it can mean fewer tears.
slides.image_prompt: Whole onions resting on a frosty shelf with ice crystals, a sharp chef's knife beside them, cool blue tones

caption:
That sting is not the smell. Cutting an onion breaks its cells and starts a chemical reaction. It makes a sulfur gas that reaches your eyes, so your tear glands flush it away.

Scientists only identified the enzyme behind it in 2002. Tip: a chilled onion can release less gas, and a sharp knife crushes fewer cells.

Send this to the friend who always cries over the cutting board. What is your own trick to stop onion tears?
